ludwig-xiv#summary: The Sun King, whose 72-year reign became the very definition of absolutism.
ludwig-xiv#text: Louis became king at the age of four and took over the government himself in 1661, after the death of his minister Mazarin. With Versailles, a standing army, and an economy directed by Colbert, he expanded the power of the crown and waged numerous wars against his neighbors. In 1685 he revoked the Edict of Nantes and forced hundreds of thousands of Huguenots to flee. The remark attributed to him that he was the state sums up his understanding of rule.
isaac-newton#summary: The founder of classical mechanics and discoverer of the law of gravitation.
isaac-newton#text: Newton taught at Cambridge and, alongside the laws of motion and the theory of gravitation, developed calculus, split white light into colors with a prism, and built a reflecting telescope. Later he headed the Royal Mint and the Royal Society. According to the Julian calendar then in use in England he was born in 1642; according to the Gregorian calendar used today, in 1643.
peter-der-grosse#role: Tsar and first Emperor of Russia
peter-der-grosse#summary: The reforming tsar who forcibly modernized Russia along Western lines.
peter-der-grosse#text: In 1697 Peter traveled through Western Europe incognito, worked in Dutch shipyards, and brought specialists back to Russia. He built up a fleet and a modern army, reformed the administration and the church, had the nobles' beards cut off, and introduced Western dress. In the Great Northern War he defeated Sweden at Poltava in 1709 and made Russia a Baltic power; in 1721 he assumed the title of emperor.
voltaire#role: Writer and philosopher of the Enlightenment
voltaire#summary: The sharp-tongued critic of intolerance, superstition, and arbitrary rule, and the most famous author of the French Enlightenment.
voltaire#text: François-Marie Arouet, who called himself Voltaire, was imprisoned in the Bastille for his mocking verses and, in exile in England, came to admire the freedom of Parliament and the science of Newton. In novels such as Candide, in plays, historical works, and thousands of letters, he fought for tolerance and the rule of law and took up the cause of victims of religious justice such as the Protestant Jean Calas. For several years he lived as a guest of Frederick II in Potsdam, but fell out with the king.
friedrich-ii-von-preussen#summary: Frederick the Great, the enlightened absolutist who made Prussia a great power.
friedrich-ii-von-preussen#text: Occupied as crown prince with the flute, philosophy, and French literature, Frederick conquered Silesia from Austria immediately after coming to the throne in 1740 and defended it in the Seven Years' War. He called himself the first servant of his state, abolished torture, granted religious tolerance, and promoted the justice system and agriculture, but held fast to noble privileges and unlimited royal power. His palace of Sanssouci in Potsdam was a meeting place for figures of the Enlightenment.
immanuel-kant#summary: The philosopher from Königsberg who defined the Enlightenment as the courage to think for oneself.
immanuel-kant#text: Kant almost never left his native city of Königsberg, where he taught as professor of logic and metaphysics. In the Critique of Pure Reason of 1781 he examined the limits of human knowledge; in his ethics he formulated the categorical imperative as a universal moral law. His essay Perpetual Peace of 1795 sketched an order of republics peacefully bound together. The motto Sapere aude, dare to use your own understanding, became the watchword of the Enlightenment.
perikles#summary: The leading politician of Athens, under whom democracy was expanded and the Acropolis was built.
perikles#text: Pericles was elected general again and again over decades and shaped the policy of Athens. He introduced daily payments so that poorer citizens too could serve in offices and courts, and he used the funds of the Delian League to build the Parthenon and other structures on the Acropolis. His circle included the sculptor Phidias and the philosopher Anaxagoras. He died in 429 BC of the plague that struck Athens at the beginning of the Peloponnesian War.
sokrates#summary: The Athenian who, through persistent questioning, turned philosophy toward human beings and right conduct.
sokrates#text: Socrates left no writings; he is known through the dialogues of his student Plato and the accounts of Xenophon. In the marketplace of Athens he drew his fellow citizens into conversations about justice, virtue, and knowledge and exposed their false certainties; his statement that he knew that he knew nothing became proverbial. His death by the cup of hemlock in 399 BC made him the symbol of the thinker who stays true to his convictions.
platon#role: Philosopher and founder of the Academy
platon#summary: A student of Socrates whose dialogues and theory of forms laid the foundations of European philosophy.
platon#text: Plato came from a distinguished Athenian family and was deeply marked by the condemnation of his teacher Socrates. Around 387 BC he founded the Academy, the first school of philosophy, which lasted almost 900 years. In dialogues such as the Republic, the Symposium, and the Phaedo he developed the doctrine of eternal forms, the allegory of the cave, and the design of a state ruled by philosophers.
aristoteles#summary: A student of Plato and teacher of Alexander who systematically ordered nearly every field of knowledge of his time.
aristoteles#text: Aristotle came from Stagira in northern Greece, studied for twenty years at Plato's Academy, and taught the young Alexander at the Macedonian court. In Athens he founded the Lyceum. His writings on logic, physics, biology, ethics, politics, rhetoric, and poetics rested on observation and the ordering of knowledge and shaped scholarship in the Islamic world and in the Christian Middle Ages for over fifteen hundred years.
alexander-der-grosse#summary: The Macedonian king who by the age of 32 ruled an empire stretching from Greece to India.
alexander-der-grosse#text: Alexander became king at the age of 20 after the murder of his father Philip II and set out in 334 BC on his campaign against Persia. In the battles of Issus and Gaugamela he defeated the Great King Darius III, conquered Egypt, Babylon, and Persepolis, and pushed as far as the Indus. He promoted the union of Greeks and Persians and founded numerous cities. His death at the age of 32 in Babylon left an empire without an heir, out of which the Hellenistic kingdoms emerged.
kyros-ii#summary: The Achaemenid king who united Persians and Medes and ruled a world empire with tolerance toward the peoples he subjected.
kyros-ii#text: Cyrus rose from ruler of a small principality to king over Medes, Lydians, and Babylonians. Unlike earlier conquerors, he left the subjected peoples their religion, language, and customs; the Cyrus Cylinder from Babylon attests to this policy. He died around 530 BC on a campaign against nomads in the east and was buried at Pasargadae, where his tomb still stands today. Greek authors such as Xenophon and the Hebrew Bible likewise portray him as a just ruler.
siddhartha-gautama#summary: A prince's son from the Himalayan foothills who, as the Buddha, the Awakened One, taught a path to liberation from suffering.
siddhartha-gautama#text: According to tradition, Siddhartha grew up sheltered in the princely house of the Shakya near Kapilavastu, until his encounter with old age, sickness, and death shook him. He left his family and the palace, tried severe asceticism, and finally found in meditation the Middle Way between indulgence and self-torment. As the Buddha he taught that greed, hatred, and ignorance cause suffering and can be overcome through right thought and action. The exact dates of his life are uncertain; scholarship places his death between 480 and 400 BC.
konfuzius#summary: China's most influential thinker, whose teaching of duty, humaneness, and education shaped the state for more than two thousand years.
konfuzius#text: Kong Qiu, Latinized as Confucius, came from the state of Lu in present-day Shandong and served for a time as an official before traveling from court to court as an itinerant teacher. He demanded that rulers govern by example rather than by punishment, and that every person fulfill his role in family and society conscientiously. His students preserved his words in the Analects, and later emperors built temples in his honor. Until 1905 Chinese officials had to pass examinations on the Confucian classics.
qin-shihuangdi#summary: The king of Qin who unified China, standardized writing and measures, and had himself buried with a terracotta army.
qin-shihuangdi#text: Ying Zheng ascended the throne of Qin at the age of thirteen and by 221 BC had subdued all rival states. As First Emperor he had roads, canals, and frontier walls built, banned divergent scripts, and, according to tradition, had books burned and scholars executed. Out of fear of death he searched for elixirs of immortality and had an enormous tomb built for himself with thousands of life-size clay soldiers, discovered near Xi'an in 1974. His dynasty outlasted him by only a few years, but his unified state endured for millennia.
ashoka#summary: The Indian great king who, after a cruel war, became a patron of Buddhism and of a policy of nonviolence.
ashoka#text: Ashoka, grandson of the empire's founder Chandragupta Maurya, ruled from about 268 to 232 BC from Pataliputra over almost all of India. After the conquest of Kalinga he repented of the bloodshed and proclaimed the dharma in edicts: respect for all living beings, religious tolerance, and care for his subjects. He had hospitals, wells, and roads built and supported Buddhist monasteries and missions, among them that of his son Mahinda in Sri Lanka. His pillars and inscriptions are among the oldest legible written records of India.
wilhelm-ii#role: Last German Emperor and King of Prussia
wilhelm-ii#summary: Led Germany into isolation through his pursuit of world power and naval armament, and lost his throne in 1918.
wilhelm-ii#text: Wilhelm II dismissed Bismarck in 1890 and pursued a world policy of colonies and a large battle fleet, which made Great Britain an opponent. His careless speeches and appearances sharpened crises, and in the July Crisis of 1914 he assured Austria-Hungary of unconditional support. During the war he increasingly lost control to the Supreme Army Command. After the November Revolution of 1918 he fled into exile in the Netherlands, where he died in 1941.
lenin#role: Revolutionary and founder of the Soviet Union
lenin#summary: Led the Bolsheviks to power in 1917 and established the first communist state.
lenin#text: Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov, who called himself Lenin, forged Russian social democracy into a tightly organized party of professional revolutionaries. After the October Revolution he made peace with Germany, distributed the land to the peasants, and secured Bolshevik rule in the civil war with the Red Army and the secret police. He died in 1924 after several strokes; his embalmed body still lies in the mausoleum on Red Square.
woodrow-wilson#summary: Led the United States into the war and designed a new world order with the Fourteen Points and the League of Nations.
woodrow-wilson#text: The former university professor Wilson became president in 1912 and was reelected in 1916 on the promise to keep the United States out of the war. After entering the war in 1917 he proclaimed the Fourteen Points, with the right of peoples to self-determination and the idea of a League of Nations. In Paris he was able to prevail only in part against the demands of France and Great Britain, and the American Senate rejected membership in the League of Nations. In 1919 he received the Nobel Peace Prize.
rosa-luxemburg#summary: An opponent of the war, cofounder of the German Communist Party, and murdered by Freikorps soldiers in 1919.
rosa-luxemburg#text: Luxemburg, who came from Poland, earned her doctorate in Zurich and became the leading theorist of the left wing of German social democracy. Because she agitated against the war, she spent almost the entire period of the war in prison. She criticized the dictatorship of the Bolsheviks with the statement that freedom is always the freedom of those who think differently. After the January uprising in Berlin she was murdered on January 15, 1919, together with Karl Liebknecht, by Freikorps soldiers.
mustafa-kemal-atatuerk#role: Founder and first President of the Republic of Turkey
mustafa-kemal-atatuerk#summary: Defender of Gallipoli, victor in the war of independence, and reformer who oriented Turkey toward the West.
mustafa-kemal-atatuerk#text: As an officer, Mustafa Kemal became known in 1915 for the successful defense of the Dardanelles against the Allies. After the defeat of the Ottoman Empire he led the resistance against the partition of Anatolia and founded the republic in 1923. As president he carried out radical reforms within a few years: civil law on the European model, the Latin alphabet, women's suffrage, and the separation of religion and state. In 1934 parliament bestowed on him the name Atatürk, father of the Turks.
sargon-von-akkad#summary: The first ruler to unite Mesopotamia into a great empire.
sargon-von-akkad#text: Sargon is said to have begun as cupbearer to the king of Kish before he founded the city of Akkad and subdued Sumer around 2334 BC. His campaigns took him as far as the Mediterranean and into the Zagros Mountains. He ruled for more than 50 years and was still revered in Mesopotamia millennia later as the model of a great king. His daughter Enheduanna is the first poet in world history known by name.
hammurapi#summary: Made Babylon the leading power of Mesopotamia and left behind the most famous collection of laws of antiquity.
hammurapi#text: Hammurabi ruled from about 1792 to 1750 BC and united all of Mesopotamia under the rule of Babylon through wars and alliances. He had canals, temples, and city walls built and saw himself as the just shepherd of his people. His code of laws regulated life in family, economy, and law and was still being copied in scribal schools centuries later.
hatschepsut#role: Female pharaoh of the New Kingdom
hatschepsut#summary: One of the few women on the Egyptian throne, who ruled as pharaoh with full royal titles.
hatschepsut#text: Hatshepsut first took over the regency for her young stepson Thutmose III and then had herself crowned pharaoh; in images she wears the ceremonial royal beard. Her roughly 20-year rule was peaceful and economically successful, and the trading expedition to the land of Punt on the Red Sea is famous. Her terraced temple at Deir el-Bahari near Thebes is among the most beautiful buildings in Egypt. After her death many of her images and names were erased.
echnaton#summary: The heretic king who raised the sun disk Aten to be Egypt's only god.
echnaton#text: Akhenaten came to the throne as Amenhotep IV and ruled for about 17 years. He moved the capital to Akhetaten and worshipped the sun disk Aten alone, thereby stripping the powerful priesthood of Amun of its power. His reform is often interpreted as an early attempt at monotheism. With his wife Nefertiti he had six daughters; his successor Tutankhamun restored the old religion.
ramses-ii#summary: Ramesses the Great ruled for 66 years, fought at Kadesh, and built the temples of Abu Simbel.
ramses-ii#text: Ramesses II came to the throne in 1279 BC and ruled longer than almost any other pharaoh. After the Battle of Kadesh he made peace with the Hittites and married a Hittite princess. He had more structures built than any other king of Egypt, among them the rock temples of Abu Simbel, the Ramesseum, and the new capital Pi-Ramesse in the Nile Delta. His mummy is preserved and is today in Cairo.
james-watt#summary: Decisively improved the steam engine and made it the motor of industrialization.
james-watt#text: Watt recognized that Thomas Newcomen's steam engine wasted a great deal of energy, and from 1765 he developed a separate condenser that cut consumption by more than half. Together with the entrepreneur Matthew Boulton he built engines that drove pumps, spinning mills, and rolling mills. The unit of power, the watt, bears his name.
karl-marx#summary: Founder of Marxism and author of the Communist Manifesto.
karl-marx#text: Born in Trier, Marx was expelled as a journalist and revolutionary from Germany, France, and Belgium and lived in London from 1849. There, with the support of Friedrich Engels, he wrote his principal work Capital, in which he analyzed the capitalist economy and predicted its downfall. His ideas shaped the labor movement and, in the 20th century, numerous states that invoked his name.
abraham-lincoln#summary: Led the United States through the Civil War, preserved the Union, and abolished slavery.
abraham-lincoln#text: Lincoln grew up in poor circumstances, trained himself as a lawyer, and became president in 1860 as the candidate of the Republicans. He prevented the division of the country, proclaimed the emancipation of the slaves in the Southern states in 1863, and in the Gettysburg Address summed up the idea of democracy as government of the people, by the people, for the people. A few days after victory he was shot on April 14, 1865, by a sympathizer of the South.
otto-von-bismarck#role: Prussian minister-president and first German chancellor
otto-von-bismarck#summary: United Germany with iron and blood and directed the policy of the empire for almost two decades.
otto-von-bismarck#text: As minister-president of Prussia from 1862, Bismarck achieved German unification through wars against Denmark, Austria, and France. As chancellor he secured peace through a system of alliances, fought Catholics and Social Democrats, and at the same time introduced the world's first state health, accident, and pension insurance. In 1890 the young Emperor Wilhelm II dismissed him.
kaiser-meiji#summary: Symbolic figure of Japan's modernization from a closed feudal state into an industrial power.
kaiser-meiji#text: Mutsuhito ascended the throne in 1867 at the age of 14 and gave his reign the name Meiji, enlightened rule. In his name the reformers moved the capital to Tokyo, introduced a constitution in 1889, and adopted Western technology, education, and military organization. The victories over China in 1895 and Russia in 1905 made Japan a great power.
marie-curie#summary: Discoverer of the elements polonium and radium and the first woman to receive a Nobel Prize.
marie-curie#text: Born in Warsaw, Maria Skłodowska studied in Paris, where, unlike in Poland, women were admitted to university. Together with her husband Pierre she investigated radioactivity and discovered two new elements in 1898. She received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903 and the one in Chemistry in 1911 and remains to this day the only person with Nobel Prizes in two natural sciences. She died from the effects of the radiation to which she had been exposed for decades.
mohammed#summary: The merchant from Mecca who, as the proclaimer of the Quran, united the Arabs under Islam.
mohammed#text: Muhammad grew up as an orphan in Mecca and worked as a caravan trader before he began around 610 to proclaim the words of God revealed to him according to Islamic belief. In Medina he built up from 622 a community that was at once a religious, legal, and political order. He emphasized the oneness of God, the equality of believers, and the duty of prayer, fasting, almsgiving, and pilgrimage. At his death in Medina in 632 almost all of Arabia was united; his life and his transmitted sayings, the hadith, remain a model and guide for Muslims to this day.
harun-ar-raschid#summary: The most famous Abbasid caliph, under whom Baghdad reached its height and who lives on as a hero of the Thousand and One Nights.
harun-ar-raschid#text: Harun al-Rashid ruled from 786 to 809 over an empire stretching from North Africa to Central Asia. He relied on the Persian family of the Barmakids as viziers, supported poets, musicians, and scholars, and laid the foundation for the library out of which the House of Wisdom grew. He exchanged embassies with Charlemagne and in 802 gave him an elephant named Abul Abbas. In the tales of the Thousand and One Nights he roams the streets of Baghdad in disguise; the historical reality of his rule, however, was also marked by revolts and the beginning decline of the empire.
ibn-sina#summary: The Persian scholar whose Canon of Medicine was for more than 600 years the most important textbook for physicians in East and West.
ibn-sina#text: Ibn Sina was born near Bukhara in present-day Uzbekistan, was considered a child prodigy, and at the age of eighteen was already treating the emir as a physician. His Canon of Medicine systematically summarized the knowledge of Greek, Persian, and Indian medicine and, translated into Latin, was taught at European universities into the 17th century. In his Book of Healing he combined the philosophy of Aristotle with Islamic thought and thereby influenced Thomas Aquinas and Scholasticism. He died in 1037 in Hamadan in Persia.
saladin#summary: The Kurdish commander who recaptured Jerusalem from the crusaders and was regarded as chivalrous even by his opponents.
saladin#text: Salah ad-Din Yusuf was born in Tikrit and rose in the service of the Syrian ruler Nur ad-Din to become vizier of Egypt, where in 1171 he brought the Shiite caliphate of the Fatimids to an end. As sultan he united Egypt, Syria, and Mesopotamia under the Ayyubid dynasty. With the victory at Hattin and the recapture of Jerusalem in 1187 he became a hero of the Islamic world; in the Third Crusade he held his ground against Richard the Lionheart. His magnanimity toward the defeated made him a legend in Europe as well. He died in Damascus in 1193 and left behind hardly any personal property.
ibn-battuta#summary: The greatest traveler of the Middle Ages, who covered some 120,000 kilometers across three continents in thirty years.
ibn-battuta#text: Ibn Battuta came from a family of legal scholars in Tangier and left his homeland at the age of 21 for the pilgrimage to Mecca. His legal training opened doors for him everywhere in the Islamic world: he served as a judge in Delhi and in the Maldives, negotiated as an envoy with the emperor of China, and visited the courts of Byzantium, the Golden Horde, and Mali. Back in Morocco he dictated his travel account, the Rihla, to the scholar Ibn Juzayy, describing landscapes, customs, rulers, and curiosities from Timbuktu to Beijing.
mahatma-gandhi#role: Leader of the Indian independence movement
mahatma-gandhi#summary: Won India's independence from Great Britain through nonviolent resistance.
mahatma-gandhi#text: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi, called Mahatma, great soul, by his followers, developed the method of nonviolent resistance as a lawyer in South Africa. In India he organized boycotts of British goods and, in 1930, the Salt March against the salt tax, and spent years in prison. The partition of the country in 1947 and the violence between Hindus and Muslims hit him hard. On January 30, 1948, he was shot by a Hindu nationalist.
mao-zedong#role: Founder and leader of the People's Republic of China
mao-zedong#summary: Led the communists to victory and ruled China for almost three decades.
mao-zedong#text: Mao rose in the civil war and on the Long March of 1934 to 1935 to become leader of the Communist Party and founded the People's Republic in 1949. His Great Leap Forward, beginning in 1958, was meant to industrialize China rapidly, but caused a famine with tens of millions of deaths. With the Cultural Revolution from 1966 he incited young people against the party and intellectuals. After his death in 1976, Deng Xiaoping opened the country to a market economy.
john-f-kennedy#summary: Mastered the Cuban Missile Crisis, launched the moon program, and was assassinated in Dallas in 1963.
john-f-kennedy#text: Kennedy was elected to office in 1960 as the youngest elected president of the United States. His 1961 invasion at the Bay of Pigs in Cuba failed, but in the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 he kept his nerve and avoided nuclear war. During his visit to West Berlin in 1963 he declared, I am a Berliner. His commitment to civil rights and the Apollo program was completed by his successors. On November 22, 1963, he was shot in Dallas.
nelson-mandela#role: Anti-apartheid fighter and first Black president of South Africa
nelson-mandela#summary: After 27 years in prison he led South Africa out of apartheid into democracy in a spirit of reconciliation.
nelson-mandela#text: The lawyer Mandela fought apartheid within the ANC, at first peacefully, and after the Sharpeville massacre of 1960 also with sabotage. In 1964 he was sentenced to life imprisonment and spent 27 years in prison, most of them on Robben Island. After his release in 1990 he negotiated the end of apartheid with President de Klerk; both received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993. As president from 1994 to 1999 he chose reconciliation over revenge.
michail-gorbatschow#role: General Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union and President of the Soviet Union
michail-gorbatschow#summary: His reforms of glasnost and perestroika made the end of the Cold War possible.
michail-gorbatschow#text: Gorbachev took over the leadership of the Soviet Union in 1985 and tried to save the rigid system through openness and restructuring. He concluded disarmament treaties with the United States, withdrew the troops from Afghanistan, and in 1989 let the Eastern European states go their own way without intervening by force. In 1990 he consented to German reunification and received the Nobel Peace Prize. In Russia he remained controversial, because the Soviet Union fell apart under him.
willy-brandt#role: Governing Mayor of Berlin and German chancellor
willy-brandt#summary: Governed Berlin when the Wall was built and, as chancellor, launched the policy of détente with the East.
willy-brandt#text: Brandt had fled from the National Socialists to Norway and in 1961, as mayor, stood at the head of the enclosed West Berlin. As the first Social Democratic chancellor from 1969 he concluded treaties with Moscow, Warsaw, and East Germany and recognized the Oder-Neisse line. His kneeling at the memorial to the Warsaw Ghetto in 1970 became a symbol of the plea for forgiveness for German crimes. In 1971 he received the Nobel Peace Prize; in 1974 he resigned over an espionage affair.
karl-der-grosse#role: King of the Franks and emperor
karl-der-grosse#summary: The Frankish ruler who united Western Europe, renewed the imperial title, and is regarded as the father of Europe.
